sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Master every hook point in ADK's execution pipeline — guardrails, caching, audit, error recovery

Day 13 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Identify all 8 ADK callback types and their exact Python signatures

- Know what each callback's return value does (skip / replace / continue / suppress)

- Use list-of-callbacks chaining with first-truthy-wins semantics

- Avoid the `{}` trap in `on_*_error` callbacks

- Build production patterns: guardrails, caching, audit logging, error recovery

sections.title: 1. Why Callbacks Matter
sections.body:
In production, a raw agent is dangerous. It will happily send your customer's credit card number to the LLM, call a `delete_user` tool because someone typed "delete me", and burn through your Gemini quota retrying the same broken request. ADK's **callback system** is the middleware layer that sits between every step of the execution pipeline, giving you a place to intercept, modify, cache, or veto before damage propagates.

The eight callback types map one-to-one to the eight decision points in the agent pipeline: entering the agent, before/after the LLM call, before/after each tool call, after the agent finishes, and when either the LLM or a tool raises. Every callback is just a Python function — no decorators, no inheritance, no DSL. You attach it by passing `before_model_callback=my_fn` (or a list) to your `LlmAgent`. The function receives a typed `CallbackContext` (or `ToolContext` for tool hooks) and may return a sentinel object (`Content`, `LlmResponse`, or `dict`) to short-circuit the pipeline.

The two killer features that distinguish ADK callbacks from "just wrapping your LLM call in a try/except" are (1) **chaining** — every callback field accepts a list, so you compose `before_model_callback=[policy_check, cache_lookup, audit_log]` and ADK invokes them in order, stopping at the first truthy return; and (2) **symmetry** — the same hook surface is exposed as `BasePlugin` methods, so you can package a callback into a reusable plugin that applies runner-wide across all agents without touching agent code. By the end of today, you'll have all eight signatures memorized and a library of patterns you can drop into any agent.

💡 Key Concept

**Callbacks are the contract between your business logic and the agent runtime.** A `before_model_callback` returning an `LlmResponse` is *literally* a cache hit — the LLM never gets called. A `before_tool_callback` returning a `dict` is *literally* a tool override — the tool function never runs. This is not a side-effect API; it is the primary mechanism for guardrails, caching, PII redaction, rate limiting, and error recovery in ADK.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts
sections.body:
### 2.1 The 8 Callback Types and Their Exact Signatures

ADK exposes exactly eight callback hooks. Each one fires at a specific point in the pipeline and receives a specific set of parameters. **Python passes these by keyword argument**, which means parameter names *must* match exactly — `def my_cb(ctx, llm_request)` will raise `TypeError: got an unexpected keyword argument 'callback_context'`. Always use the canonical names.

| # | Field on `LlmAgent` | Required parameter names | Return type | Effect of non-`None` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `before_agent_callback` | `callback_context` | `Optional[Content]` | Returning `Content` **skips the agent's run**; that content becomes the agent's output |
| 2 | `after_agent_callback` | `callback_context` | `Optional[Content]` | Returning `Content` **replaces** the agent's final output |
| 3 | `before_model_callback` | `callback_context`, `llm_request` | `Optional[LlmResponse]` | Returning `LlmResponse` **skips the LLM call** (caching, guardrails) |
| 4 | `after_model_callback` | `callback_context`, `llm_response` | `Optional[LlmResponse]` | Returning `LlmResponse` **replaces** the model's response |
| 5 | `before_tool_callback` | `tool`, `args`, `tool_context` | `Optional[dict]` | Returning a `dict` **skips tool execution** (override). ⚠️ `{}` also overrides! |
| 6 | `after_tool_callback` | `tool`, `args`, `tool_context`, `tool_response` | `Optional[dict]` | Returning a `dict` **replaces** `tool_response` |
| 7 | `on_model_error_callback` | `callback_context`, `llm_request`, `error` | `Optional[LlmResponse]` | Returning `LlmResponse` **suppresses the exception** |
| 8 | `on_tool_error_callback` | `tool`, `args`, `tool_context`, `error` | `Optional[dict]` | Returning a `dict` **suppresses the exception** and becomes the tool result |

⚠️ Important

**Parameter name pitfall.** Python passes callback arguments by keyword. Writing `def guard(ctx, llm_request)` (using `ctx` instead of `callback_context`) raises `TypeError: guard() got an unexpected keyword argument 'callback_context'` at runtime — not at registration. Always use the exact names: `callback_context`, `llm_request`, `llm_response`, `tool`, `args`, `tool_context`, `tool_response`, `error`.

### 2.2 The Pipeline — Where Each Callback Fires

The eight hooks are not scattered randomly; they sit at predictable points in the agent's request→response loop. Internalize this diagram — every debugging session about "why didn't my callback fire?" comes down to knowing which gate you placed it at.

```
                       ADK CALLBACK PIPELINE (8 HOOK POINTS)
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                          │
│   User message                                                           │
│        │                                                                 │
│        ▼                                                                 │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   returns Content?  → YES: skip agent run     │
│   │ ① before_agent_cb   │                       NO:  continue            │
│   └──────────┬──────────┘                                                │
│              ▼                                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   returns LlmResponse? → YES: skip LLM call   │
│   │ ② before_model_cb   │   (cache hit / guardrail)                      │
│   └──────────┬──────────┘                                                │
│              ▼                                                           │
│        ┌───────────┐    raises Exception?                                │
│        │   LLM     │──────┐                                              │
│        └─────┬─────┘      ▼                                              │
│              │       ┌──────────────────────┐                            │
│              │       │ ⑦ on_model_error_cb  │ returns LlmResponse?       │
│              │       │    (suppress raise)  │  → YES: use it             │
│              │       └──────────────────────┘  → NO:  propagate          │
│              ▼                                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   returns LlmResponse? → YES: replace resp    │
│   │ ③ after_model_cb    │                                                │
│   └──────────┬──────────┘                                                │
│              ▼                                                           │
│        Tool call?  YES ──┐    NO ──► ┌─────────────────────┐             │
│                          │           │ ⑧ after_agent_cb    │             │
│                          ▼           │   (replace output)  │             │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐            └─────────────────────┘             │
│   │ ④ before_tool_cb    │ returns dict? → YES: skip tool exec            │
│   │   (cache / override)│                (returns `{}` also overrides!)  │
│   └──────────┬──────────┘                                                │
│              ▼                                                           │
│        ┌───────────┐    raises Exception?                                │
│        │  TOOL     │──────┐                                              │
│        └─────┬─────┘      ▼                                              │
│              │       ┌──────────────────────┐                            │
│              │       │ ⑨ on_tool_error_cb   │ returns dict?              │
│              │       │    (suppress raise)  │  → YES: become result      │
│              │       └──────────────────────┘  → NO:  propagate          │
│              ▼                                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   returns dict? → YES: replace tool_response  │
│   │ ⑤ after_tool_cb     │                                                │
│   └──────────┬──────────┘                                                │
│              │                                                           │
│              └──► loop back to LLM                                       │
│                                                                          │
│  Chaining: every callback field accepts a LIST. ADK invokes in order,    │
│  stops at the first truthy return.  on_*_error stops on ANY non-None     │
│  return (including `{}`!).                                               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 2.3 Chaining: Lists of Callbacks

Every callback field accepts either a single function *or a list of functions*. When you pass a list, ADK invokes each one in order and **stops at the first truthy return**. This is the same "first-wins" semantics as Python's `or` operator: `policy_check() or cache_lookup() or audit_log()`.

For `before_*` and `after_*` callbacks, "truthy" means a non-`None` value (an `LlmResponse`, a `dict`, a `Content`). For `on_*_error` callbacks, the rule is stricter: **any non-`None` return stops the chain, including an empty dict `{}`**. This is because error callbacks need a way to say "I handled it, but the result is empty" — so the framework treats `{}` as a valid suppression signal, not as "I did nothing".

```
LIST-OF-CALLBACKS CHAINING (first truthy wins)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  before_model_callback = [policy_check, cache_lookup, audit_log]

  policy_check  →  None            ← continue chain
       │
       ▼
  cache_lookup →  LlmResponse(...) ← STOP!  skip remaining + skip LLM
       │
       ▼ (audit_log NEVER runs)

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  on_model_error_callback = [retry_smaller, log_error, fallback_text]

  retry_smaller →  None            ← continue chain (didn't handle)
       │
       ▼
  log_error     →  {}              ← STOP!  Empty dict counts as non-None
       │                              for error callbacks. Suppresses raise
       ▼ (fallback_text NEVER runs)   and becomes the "result".

  ⚠️  This is the most common callback bug. Returning {} to "do nothing"
      in an error callback actually swallows the exception silently.
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

🚀 Pro Tip

Compose guardrails as **ordered lists**, with the cheapest check first. `[rate_limit, profanity_filter, pii_redactor]` runs rate limiting (an in-memory dict lookup) before the more expensive regex scan for PII. If rate limit returns a "429" `LlmResponse`, the other two never run — saving CPU on every blocked request.

### 2.4 Async vs Sync

ADK's runner is async, but your callbacks don't have to be. A callback can be a plain `def` or an `async def` — ADK detects which and `await`s accordingly. If your callback does I/O (calling a policy API, reading from Redis, fetching a cache row), make it `async def` so it doesn't block the event loop. If it does pure CPU work (regex, dict lookup), `def` is fine.

Mixing is allowed within a chain: `[sync_rate_limit, async_pii_redactor]` works. ADK awaits each one appropriately. Note that for `async def` callbacks, you cannot use synchronous blocking calls like `time.sleep()` — use `await asyncio.sleep()` instead, or you'll freeze the event loop for all agents sharing it.

### 2.5 Imports and the `CallbackContext` Object

All the types you need live in a handful of stable modules. The most common import block for a callbacks file looks like this:

```python
# Standard callback imports
from typing import Any, Optional
from copy import deepcopy

from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.agents.callback_context import CallbackContext
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext
from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool
from google.adk.models import LlmRequest, LlmResponse
from google.genai import types
```

**Output**

```text
(no output — imports succeed silently)
```

The `CallbackContext` object exposes everything you need to make decisions inside a callback:

- **`callback_context.agent_name`** — the agent's name (useful for shared callbacks that behave differently per agent)
- **`callback_context.invocation_id`** — a UUID for the current run (correlate logs across an entire turn)
- **`callback_context.state`** — a dict-like view of session state, with prefix scoping (`user:`, `app:`, `temp:`). You can read **and write** — writing mutates the session's state delta for this event.
- **`callback_context.events`** — the full event history for this session so far (read-only)
- **`callback_context.session`** — the underlying `Session` object (id, user_id, app_name, last_update_time)
- **`callback_context._invocation_context`** — escape hatch for advanced use (rarely needed)

For tool callbacks, `ToolContext` adds: `tool_context.function_call_id` (correlates request→response), `tool_context.actions` (set `transfer_to_agent`, `escalate`, `state_delta`), and `tool_context.artifact` / `tool_context.memory` shortcuts.

💡 Key Concept

**State mutation in callbacks is the killer feature.** A `before_model_callback` can write `callback_context.state["temp:rate_limit_count"] += 1` and that increment becomes part of the event's `state_delta` — persisted to the session service, visible to the next callback in the chain, and replayed on session resume. This is how you implement rate limiting, multi-turn guardrail counters, and audit trails without any external database.

### 2.6 Plugins vs Callbacks

`BasePlugin` (from `google.adk.plugins`) provides the **exact same hook surface** (`before_agent_callback`, `after_agent_callback`, `before_model_callback`, `after_model_callback`, `before_tool_callback`, `after_tool_callback`, plus runner-wide `before_run_callback` / `after_run_callback`) but at **runner-wide granularity**. A plugin applies to every agent the runner executes; a callback applies to one agent.

Use **callbacks** when the logic is specific to one agent (e.g., a guardrail that only applies to the billing agent). Use **plugins** when the logic is universal (e.g., a `LoggingPlugin` that should log every agent in the system, or a `BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin` that ships every event to BigQuery for analytics). You register plugins at runner construction time:

```python
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.plugins import BasePlugin
runner = Runner(agent=root, session_service=svc, plugins=[LoggingPlugin()])
```

ADK v2.7.0 ships two production plugins worth knowing: `ReflectAndRetryModelPlugin` (added in v2.6.0 — when the model returns a malformed response, the plugin asks the model to reflect on its error and retry) and `BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin` (added in v2.7.0 — install `google-adk[bigquery-analytics]`).

🚀 Pro Tip

**Rule of thumb:** Start with callbacks during development — they're easier to attach/detach per-agent. Promote to a plugin when the same callback gets copy-pasted into 3+ agents. The plugin contract is identical, so promotion is a mechanical refactor.

sections.title: 3. Visual Diagram — Pipeline + Callback Hook Points
sections.body:
The Mermaid diagram below shows the runtime decision flow with every callback hook called out. Compare it with the matplotlib chart on the next cell — both encode the same pipeline, but the matplotlib chart additionally lists the exact signatures.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
U[User Message] --> R[Runner]
R --> S[(Session Service)]
S --> AG[Agent]
AG --> BM{before_model
callback?}
BM -->|None| LLM[LLM Call]
BM -->|LlmResponse| SKIP[Skip LLM]
LLM --> AM{after_model
callback?}
SKIP --> AM
AM --> TC{Tool call?}
TC -->|Yes| BT{before_tool
callback?}
BT -->|None| TOOL[Execute Tool]
BT -->|dict| SKIP_TOOL[Skip tool]
TOOL --> AT[after_tool callback]
SKIP_TOOL --> AT
AT --> LLM
TC -->|No| FINAL[Final Response Event]
AT --> LLM
FINAL --> S
style R fill:#1A73E8,color:#fff
style AG fill:#34A853,color:#fff
style LLM fill:#FBBC04,color:#202124
style FINAL fill:#EA4335,color:#fff
```

### The 8-callback map (pre-generated PNG)

```python
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename="images/day13_callbacks_map.png"))
```

The red boxes (`before_*`) are *skip-the-step* hooks — returning a value bypasses the downstream step entirely. The green boxes (`after_*`) are *replace-the-result* hooks — returning a value substitutes the result the step would have produced. The purple boxes (`on_*_error`) fire *only* when the step raises, and returning a value suppresses the exception. The yellow box is the LLM call itself, the only step that's not a hook.

Example 1: before_model_callback Guardrail

Block queries containing the word 'BLOCK' — the LLM is never called

The simplest production guardrail: scan the user's latest message before it reaches the LLM, and return a canned response if a forbidden keyword is present. Because we return an `LlmResponse`, the LLM call is **completely skipped** — no token cost, no latency, no quota usage. This is exactly how you implement profanity filters, PII redaction gates, and topic restrictions in production.

Note two subtle points in the code below. First, the callback receives `llm_request: LlmRequest` — by mutating it in place (e.g., prepending text to the system instruction) and returning `None`, you can **modify** the request without skipping the call. Returning a non-`None` `LlmResponse` is what triggers the skip. Second, the callback inspects `llm_request.contents[-1]` to find the last user message — the contents list is the full conversation history, and the last item with `role == "user"` is the current turn.

```python
# agent.py — Example 1: before_model_callback guardrail
from typing import Optional
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.agents.callback_context import CallbackContext
from google.adk.models import LlmRequest, LlmResponse
from google.genai import types

def block_keyword_guardrail(
    callback_context: CallbackContext,
    llm_request: LlmRequest,
) -> Optional[LlmResponse]:
    """Block queries containing the word 'BLOCK'.

    Returning a LlmResponse skips the LLM call entirely —
    zero tokens spent, zero latency.
    """
    invocation_id = callback_context.invocation_id
    agent_name = callback_context.agent_name
    print(f"[guardrail] agent={agent_name} invocation={invocation_id[:8]}")

    # Inspect the last user message in the contents list
    if not llm_request.contents:
        return None  # nothing to check
    last = llm_request.contents[-1]
    if last.role != "user" or not last.parts:
        return None

    user_text = (last.parts[0].text or "").upper()
    if "BLOCK" in user_text:
        print("[guardrail] 🚫 BLOCK keyword detected — skipping LLM call")
        return LlmResponse(
            content=types.Content(
                role="model",
                parts=[types.Part(
                    text="I'm sorry, this query has been blocked by the "
                         "content guardrail. Please rephrase your request."
                )],
            )
        )
    return None  # all clear — let the LLM run

root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="guarded_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="You are a helpful assistant.",
    before_model_callback=block_keyword_guardrail,
)

print(f"Agent '{root_agent.name}' registered guardrail: block_keyword_guardrail")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent 'guarded_agent' registered guardrail: block_keyword_guardrail
```

### Simulated run

Below is what you'd see if you sent two prompts to this agent via `adk run`. The first contains the forbidden keyword and never touches the LLM; the second is clean and gets a normal response. Note the absence of a "Calling LLM" log line on the blocked turn — the guardrail truly short-circuited the pipeline.

```python
# Simulated run output
import asyncio
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.adk.events import Event
from google.genai import types

async def demo():
    session_service = InMemorySessionService()
    session = await session_service.create_session(
        app_name="demo", user_id="user1"
    )
    runner = Runner(
        agent=root_agent,
        app_name="demo",
        session_service=session_service,
    )

    for prompt in [
        "Please BLOCK this request immediately.",
        "What is the capital of France?",
    ]:
        print(f"\n>>> USER: {prompt}")
        msg = types.Content(
            role="user",
            parts=[types.Part(text=prompt)],
        )
        async for event in runner.run_async(
            user_id=session.user_id,
            session_id=session.id,
            new_message=msg,
        ):
            if event.is_final_response() and event.content:
                print(f"<<< MODEL: {event.content.parts[0].text}")

# In a real notebook, you'd `await demo()`. We print the expected output:
print("""
>>> USER: Please BLOCK this request immediately.
[guardrail] agent=guarded_agent invocation=a1b2c3d4
[guardrail] 🚫 BLOCK keyword detected — skipping LLM call
<<< MODEL: I'm sorry, this query has been blocked by the
           content guardrail. Please rephrase your request.

>>> USER: What is the capital of France?
[guardrail] agent=guarded_agent invocation=e5f6g7h8
<<< MODEL: The capital of France is Paris.
""")
```

**Output**

```text
>>> USER: Please BLOCK this request immediately.\n[guardrail] agent=guarded_agent invocation=a1b2c3d4\n[guardrail] 🚫 BLOCK keyword detected — skipping LLM call\n<<< MODEL: I'm sorry, this query has been blocked by the\n           content guardrail. Please rephrase your request.\n\n>>> USER: What is the capital of France?\n[guardrail] agent=guarded_agent invocation=e5f6g7h8\n<<< MODEL: The capital of France is Paris.\n
```

💡 Key Concept

A returning-`LlmResponse` `before_model_callback` is the most cost-effective pattern in ADK. Every blocked request is a request you didn't pay for. In a high-traffic support agent, a well-tuned guardrail can cut LLM costs by 20–40% by intercepting out-of-scope queries before they ever reach the model.

Example 2: after_tool_callback Response Modifier

Annotate capital_city tool responses with a contextual note

Sometimes you don't want to skip a tool — you want to *enrich* its result. `after_tool_callback` fires after the tool function returns, receives the tool's response dict, and may return a *replacement* dict. This is perfect for adding compliance footnotes, redacting sensitive fields, normalizing units, or injecting caching metadata.

The signature is `after_tool_callback(tool, args, tool_context, tool_response)` — note `tool` (a `BaseTool`), `args` (the dict of arguments the LLM passed), `tool_context` (a `ToolContext`), and `tool_response` (the dict the tool returned). Use `tool.name` to gate behavior to specific tools, and **always `deepcopy` before mutating** — `tool_response` is the live object, and mutating it in place is a footgun.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: after_tool_callback modifier
from copy import deepcopy
from typing import Any, Optional
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext
from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool

def get_capital_city(country: str) -> dict:
    """Returns the capital city of a country.

    Args:
        country: Country name, e.g. 'France' or 'Japan'.
    """
    capitals = {
        "France": "Paris",
        "Japan": "Tokyo",
        "USA": "Washington, D.C.",
        "Brazil": "Brasília",
    }
    return {
        "country": country,
        "result": capitals.get(country, "Unknown"),
        "source": "static_lookup_table",
    }

def annotate_capital_response(
    tool: BaseTool,
    args: dict[str, Any],
    tool_context: ToolContext,
    tool_response: dict,
) -> Optional[dict]:
    """Append a contextual note to capital_city responses.

    Fires for every tool — we gate on tool.name to scope it.
    Returns a *replacement* dict; returning None keeps original.
    """
    if tool.name != "get_capital_city":
        return None

    # Deepcopy — never mutate tool_response in place
    modified = deepcopy(tool_response)
    country = modified.get("country", "")
    result = modified.get("result", "")

    # Add an explanatory note for specific countries
    notes = {
        "USA": " (the capital of the United States, not New York)",
        "Brazil": " (note: Brazil's capital moved from Rio to Brasília in 1960)",
        "Australia": " (note: Australia's capital is Canberra, not Sydney)",
    }
    if country in notes:
        modified["result"] = f"{result}{notes[country]}"
        modified["note_added_by_callback"] = True
        print(f"[after_tool] Annotated response for {country}")
        return modified

    # Add a generic source citation
    modified["result"] = f"{result} (sourced via ADK callback audit)"
    modified["note_added_by_callback"] = True
    return modified

root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="geography_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction=(
        "You answer geography questions. Use the get_capital_city tool "
        "to look up capitals. Always cite the source you saw in the result."
    ),
    tools=[get_capital_city],
    after_tool_callback=annotate_capital_response,
)

print(f"Agent '{root_agent.name}' — after_tool_callback registered")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent 'geography_agent' — after_tool_callback registered\n
```

### Simulated run

The callback fires *after* every tool call, but only modifies the result when the tool is `get_capital_city`. The LLM then sees the *modified* dict in its `function_response` part — meaning the LLM's final answer will reflect the annotation. This is how you transparently enrich tool outputs without changing tool implementations.

```python
# Simulated run
print("""
>>> USER: What is the capital of the USA?
[after_tool] Annotated response for USA
<<< MODEL: The capital of the USA is Washington, D.C.
           (the capital of the United States, not New York).
           Sourced via ADK callback audit.

>>> USER: What is the capital of Brazil?
[after_tool] Annotated response for Brazil
<<< MODEL: The capital of Brazil is Brasília
           (note: Brazil's capital moved from Rio to Brasília in 1960).
           Sourced via ADK callback audit.
""")
```

**Output**

```text
>>> USER: What is the capital of the USA?\n[after_tool] Annotated response for USA\n<<< MODEL: The capital of the USA is Washington, D.C.\n           (the capital of the United States, not New York).\n           Sourced via ADK callback audit.\n\n>>> USER: What is the capital of Brazil?\n[after_tool] Annotated response for Brazil\n<<< MODEL: The capital of Brazil is Brasília\n           (note: Brazil's capital moved from Rio to Brasília in 1960).\n           Sourced via ADK callback audit.\n
```

🚀 Pro Tip

Use `after_tool_callback` for **PII redaction** in reverse: if a tool returns a credit card number, the callback can mask it (`"**** **** **** 4242"`) before the LLM sees it. The LLM never logs the raw number — only the masked version. This is more reliable than prompt-engineering "don't reveal card numbers" because it's enforced at the framework level.

Example 3: Caching with before_tool_callback

Skip expensive tool calls by returning cached results keyed on args

`before_tool_callback` returning a `dict` skips the tool entirely and uses the returned dict as the tool's result. This is the canonical pattern for caching: check a cache keyed on `(tool.name, args)`, return the cached entry if present, otherwise return `None` to let the tool run — and use `after_tool_callback` (or just write the cache inside the tool itself) to populate the cache for next time.

**Critical footgun:** returning `{}` (empty dict) *also* overrides — it becomes the tool's response. To express "I have no opinion, let the tool run", you must return `None`. Many beginners write `return {}` thinking it means "no override" and then spend hours debugging why their tool silently returns empty.

```python
# agent.py — Example 3: Caching with before_tool_callback
import hashlib
import json
import time
from copy import deepcopy
from typing import Any, Optional
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext
from google.adk.tools.base_tool import BaseTool

# In-memory cache: {(tool_name, args_hash): (timestamp, response)}
_TOOL_CACHE: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[float, dict]] = {}
CACHE_TTL_SECONDS = 60.0  # 1 minute

def _args_hash(args: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    """Stable hash of tool args (sorted keys, JSON-serialized)."""
    canonical = json.dumps(args, sort_keys=True, default=str)
    return hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]

def expensive_stock_price(ticker: str) -> dict:
    """Fetch a stock price (simulated slow API call).

    Args:
        ticker: Stock ticker symbol, e.g. 'GOOGL' or 'AAPL'.
    """
    print(f"[tool] LIVE API CALL for {ticker}")
    time.sleep(0.8)  # simulate network latency
    mock_prices = {"GOOGL": 142.65, "AAPL": 198.45, "MSFT": 415.20}
    return {
        "ticker": ticker,
        "price_usd": mock_prices.get(ticker, 100.00),
        "currency": "USD",
        "fetched_at": time.time(),
    }

def cache_lookup(
    tool: BaseTool,
    args: dict[str, Any],
    tool_context: ToolContext,
) -> Optional[dict]:
    """Return cached response if present and not expired.

    Returning a dict (even {}) SKIPS the tool — must return None
    to let the tool actually execute.
    """
    key = (tool.name, _args_hash(args))
    if key in _TOOL_CACHE:
        cached_at, cached_response = _TOOL_CACHE[key]
        age = time.time() - cached_at
        if age < CACHE_TTL_SECONDS:
            print(f"[cache] HIT  tool={tool.name} age={age:.2f}s")
            # Deepcopy so callers can mutate without polluting cache
            return deepcopy(cached_response)
        else:
            print(f"[cache] EXPIRED tool={tool.name} age={age:.2f}s")
            del _TOOL_CACHE[key]
    print(f"[cache] MISS tool={tool.name}")
    return None  # ← critical: must be None, NOT {}

def cache_store(
    tool: BaseTool,
    args: dict[str, Any],
    tool_context: ToolContext,
    tool_response: dict,
) -> Optional[dict]:
    """Populate the cache after a real tool call."""
    key = (tool.name, _args_hash(args))
    _TOOL_CACHE[key] = (time.time(), deepcopy(tool_response))
    print(f"[cache] STORED tool={tool.name}")
    return None  # don't modify the response

root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="stock_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="You fetch stock prices. Use expensive_stock_price.",
    tools=[expensive_stock_price],
    # Chained callbacks: check cache first, fall back to live call
    before_tool_callback=[cache_lookup],
    after_tool_callback=[cache_store],
)

print(f"Agent '{root_agent.name}' — caching enabled, TTL={CACHE_TTL_SECONDS}s")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent 'stock_agent' — caching enabled, TTL=60.0s\n
```

### Simulated run — three calls, one live API hit

Watch the second call: same args, cache HIT, tool *never executes*. The third call (different ticker) misses and triggers a fresh live call. Note how the chained `before_tool_callback=[cache_lookup]` and `after_tool_callback=[cache_store]` cooperate — the lookup gate prevents execution, and the store hook populates the cache when execution *does* happen.

```python
# Simulated run
print("""
>>> USER: What's the price of GOOGL?
[cache] MISS tool=expensive_stock_price
[tool] LIVE API CALL for GOOGL
[cache] STORED tool=expensive_stock_price
<<< MODEL: GOOGL is currently trading at $142.65.

>>> USER: And GOOGL again, just to confirm?
[cache] HIT  tool=expensive_stock_price age=2.31s
<<< MODEL: GOOGL is currently trading at $142.65. (cached, 2.3s old)

>>> USER: What about AAPL?
[cache] MISS tool=expensive_stock_price
[tool] LIVE API CALL for AAPL
[cache] STORED tool=expensive_stock_price
<<< MODEL: AAPL is currently trading at $198.45.
""")
```

**Output**

```text
>>> USER: What's the price of GOOGL?\n[cache] MISS tool=expensive_stock_price\n[tool] LIVE API CALL for GOOGL\n[cache] STORED tool=expensive_stock_price\n<<< MODEL: GOOGL is currently trading at $142.65.\n\n>>> USER: And GOOGL again, just to confirm?\n[cache] HIT  tool=expensive_stock_price age=2.31s\n<<< MODEL: GOOGL is currently trading at $142.65. (cached, 2.3s old)\n\n>>> USER: What about AAPL?\n[cache] MISS tool=expensive_stock_price\n[tool] LIVE API CALL for AAPL\n[cache] STORED tool=expensive_stock_price\n<<< MODEL: AAPL is currently trading at $198.45.\n
```

⚠️ Important

**The `{}` footgun in `before_tool_callback`.** Returning `{}` is NOT the same as returning `None`. A `dict` (any dict, including empty) becomes the tool's response and skips the tool call entirely. If you're writing a "passthrough" callback that sometimes overrides but usually doesn't, end with an explicit `return None` — never `return {}`.

Example 4: Error Recovery with on_model_error_callback

Suppress model exceptions and fall back to a canned response

Production models fail. Rate limits, transient 5xxs, malformed responses, content-policy triggers — they all bubble up as exceptions inside the LLM call. Without an `on_model_error_callback`, the exception propagates to the runner, which surfaces it to the user as a 500. With one, you can suppress the exception and substitute a graceful fallback.

The signature is `on_model_error_callback(callback_context, llm_request, error)`. The third arg `error` is the exception that was raised. Inspect its type — `google.genai.errors.ClientError` for quota/429, `ValueError` for malformed responses, etc. — and decide whether to suppress or re-raise. **Returning `LlmResponse` suppresses the exception**; returning `None` (or `{}`!) lets it propagate. This is the inverse of `before_*` / `after_*` callbacks, where `None` means "continue normally".

```python
# agent.py — Example 4: on_model_error_callback recovery
import time
from typing import Optional
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import LlmAgent
from google.adk.agents.callback_context import CallbackContext
from google.adk.models import LlmRequest, LlmResponse
from google.genai import types

# Track failure counts for circuit-breaker behavior
_failure_counts: dict[str, int] = {}
_last_failure_ts: dict[str, float] = {}

def graceful_model_recovery(
    callback_context: CallbackContext,
    llm_request: LlmRequest,
    error: Exception,
) -> Optional[LlmResponse]:
    """Recover from LLM exceptions with tiered fallbacks.

    Strategies by error type:
      - Rate-limit / quota errors     → canned "try again later" response
      - Malformed response errors     → retry with simpler instruction
      - Repeated failures (>=3)       → circuit-break to maintenance message
      - Anything else                 → let it propagate (return None)

    IMPORTANT: returning ANY non-None LlmResponse suppresses the raise.
    Be deliberate — silent swallowing hides real bugs.
    """
    agent_name = callback_context.agent_name
    now = time.time()

    # Update failure tracking
    _failure_counts[agent_name] = _failure_counts.get(agent_name, 0) + 1
    _last_failure_ts[agent_name] = now
    count = _failure_counts[agent_name]
    print(f"[on_model_error] agent={agent_name} failure #{count} error={type(error).__name__}: {error}")

    # Circuit breaker: 3+ failures in 60s → maintenance message
    if count >= 3:
        print("[on_model_error] 🔌 Circuit breaker tripped — returning maintenance message")
        return LlmResponse(
            content=types.Content(
                role="model",
                parts=[types.Part(
                    text="I'm experiencing technical difficulties right now. "
                         "Please try again in a few minutes, or contact "
                         "support if the issue persists."
                )],
            )
        )

    # Quota / rate-limit errors → "try again later"
    error_str = str(error).lower()
    if "quota" in error_str or "rate" in error_str or "429" in error_str:
        print("[on_model_error] ⏳ Rate limited — returning retry message")
        return LlmResponse(
            content=types.Content(
                role="model",
                parts=[types.Part(
                    text="I'm currently handling too many requests. "
                         "Please wait a moment and try again."
                )],
            )
        )

    # Malformed response (e.g. invalid JSON from model) → simple fallback
    if "json" in error_str or "decode" in error_str or "parse" in error_str:
        print("[on_model_error] 📝 Malformed response — returning fallback text")
        return LlmResponse(
            content=types.Content(
                role="model",
                parts=[types.Part(
                    text="I understood your request but had trouble "
                         "formatting my response. Could you rephrase?"
                )],
            )
        )

    # Unknown error → let it propagate (don't swallow silently)
    print("[on_model_error] ❓ Unknown error — propagating")
    return None

root_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="resilient_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="You are a helpful assistant.",
    on_model_error_callback=graceful_model_recovery,
)

# Simulate resetting the failure counter between tests
_failure_counts.clear()

print(f"Agent '{root_agent.name}' — on_model_error_callback registered")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent 'resilient_agent' — on_model_error_callback registered\n
```

### Simulated run — three different errors, three different responses

The first error is a rate-limit (transient, common); the second is a JSON parse failure (model hallucinated broken JSON); the third is a circuit-breaker trip after the failure counter hits 3. Note how each invocation increments `_failure_counts[agent_name]` — this counter lives in module scope and would persist across invocations on the same runner, which is what makes the circuit-breaker behavior work.

```python
# Simulated run — three different errors, three different recoveries
print("""
>>> USER: Summarize this 10,000-word document.
[on_model_error] agent=resilient_agent failure #1 error=ClientError: 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
[on_model_error] ⏳ Rate limited — returning retry message
<<< MODEL: I'm currently handling too many requests. Please wait a moment and try again.

>>> USER: Generate a JSON config with 50 nested fields.
[on_model_error] agent=resilient_agent failure #2 error=ValueError: Invalid JSON: unexpected token
[on_model_error] 📝 Malformed response — returning fallback text
<<< MODEL: I understood your request but had trouble formatting my response. Could you rephrase?

>>> USER: One more try.
[on_model_error] agent=resilient_agent failure #3 error=ClientError: 503 UNAVAILABLE
[on_model_error] 🔌 Circuit breaker tripped — returning maintenance message
<<< MODEL: I'm experiencing technical difficulties right now. Please try again in a few minutes,
           or contact support if the issue persists.
""")
```

**Output**

```text
>>> USER: Summarize this 10,000-word document.\n[on_model_error] agent=resilient_agent failure #1 error=ClientError: 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED\n[on_model_error] ⏳ Rate limited — returning retry message\n<<< MODEL: I'm currently handling too many requests. Please wait a moment and try again.\n\n>>> USER: Generate a JSON config with 50 nested fields.\n[on_model_error] agent=resilient_agent failure #2 error=ValueError: Invalid JSON: unexpected token\n[on_model_error] 📝 Malformed response — returning fallback text\n<<< MODEL: I understood your request but had trouble formatting my response. Could you rephrase?\n\n>>> USER: One more try.\n[on_model_error] agent=resilient_agent failure #3 error=ClientError: 503 UNAVAILABLE\n[on_model_error] 🔌 Circuit breaker tripped — returning maintenance message\n<<< MODEL: I'm experiencing technical difficulties right now. Please try again in a few minutes,\n           or contact support if the issue persists.\n
```

🚀 Pro Tip

For automated retry with exponential backoff, use the built-in **`ReflectAndRetryModelPlugin`** (v2.6.0+) instead of writing your own. When the model returns a malformed response, the plugin asks the model to *reflect on its own error* and retry — often succeeding on the second attempt without any user-visible failure. Register it as a plugin: `Runner(agent=root, session_service=svc, plugins=[ReflectAndRetryModelPlugin()])`.

⚠️ Important

**Don't use `on_model_error_callback` to swallow *every* exception.** Silent error suppression is the #1 cause of "the agent just stopped working" production incidents. Reserve error callbacks for *expected, recoverable* failure modes (rate limits, transient 5xxs, malformed JSON). For unexpected errors, return `None` and let the runner surface them — your monitoring will thank you.

diagrams.title: Where ADK callbacks fire
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  BA["before_agent"] --> BM["before_model"] --> M["Model call"] --> AM["after_model"]
  AM --> BT["before_tool"] --> T["Tool run"] --> AT["after_tool"]
  AT --> BM
  AM --> AA["after_agent"]
diagrams.explain: Callbacks are hooks around the three expensive things an agent does: run an **agent**, call the **model**, run a **tool**. Returning a value from a *before_* callback **skips** the real call (use it for guardrails, caching or mocking); *after_* callbacks can inspect or rewrite the result (redaction, logging, metrics).

sections.title: Day 13 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **ADK exposes 8 callback types**, each at a specific pipeline gate: before/after agent, before/after model, before/after tool, and on-model/tool-error

- **Parameter names must match exactly** — Python passes by keyword. `def cb(ctx, llm_request)` raises `TypeError` at runtime; use `callback_context`

- **Returning a sentinel value short-circuits the pipeline**: `LlmResponse` skips the LLM, `dict` overrides the tool, `Content` skips/replaces the agent

- **Every callback field accepts a list** — ADK invokes in order, stops at first truthy return (first-wins)

- **`on_*_error` callbacks stop on ANY non-None return, including `{}`** — never return `{}` to mean "I did nothing"

- **`before_tool_callback` returning `{}` ALSO overrides (becomes the tool result) — return `None` to let the tool run**

- **Callbacks may be `def` or `async def` — ADK awaits either; use async for I/O-bound hooks (Redis lookups, HTTP policy calls)**

- **`BasePlugin` provides the same hooks at runner-wide granularity** — promote callbacks to plugins when the same logic applies to every agent
